newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan firms' profits seen growing at slower pace.
newsitem.headline: Japan firms' profits seen growing at slower pace.

text.p: Profits for Japan's top companies will not grow as fast as predicted earlier this year, several research institutes said on Friday.

"With the yen's weaker trend and Japan's economic recovery still continuing, some industries are performing well but others are not," Nomura Research Institute said in its latest quarterly study on corporate earnings.

"Earnings in the information and telecommunications industries are improving, and in the manufacturing sector we have raised our earnings forecast for car makers. But we have revised down our earnings forecasts for the chemical and steel industries," it said.
Nomura Research expects earnings at major companies to grow by 7.8 percent in 1996/97 ending March, compared with the previous fiscal year, down slightly from its June estimate of 7.9 percent.

Nikko Research Center, which also released its quarterly report on Friday, said negative factors such as slumping semiconductor prices and lower basic material prices would more than offset positive factors such as robust demand for information equipment and an expected rise in earnings in the car industry.
Nikko Research said it saw large Japanese companies' profits in 1996/97 increasing 7.2 percent from a year ago, down from its previous forecast of 8.6 percent.

Major research institutes Daiwa Institute of Research and Yamaichi Research Institute of Securities and Economics also revised down their earnings forecasts for 1996/97 in reports released on Thursday.
The revisions were due to a decline in semiconductor prices and persistently high inventory levels in the basic materials sector, they said.
Daiwa Institute lowered the rate of profit growth in 1996/97 by 0.9 percentage point to 6.8 percent. Yamaichi cut the growth in 1996/97 by 1.2 percentage point to 8.1 percent.
The four research institutes are affiliated with Japan's four largest securities houses.
Other securities house-affiliated research institutes announced quarterly reports this week as well.

Some also revised down their 1996/97 profit forecasts but others raised them, saying the yen's decline and robust demand for cars and computer-related products would have a larger impact on corporate earnings than negative factors.
Kankaku Research Institute, for example, revised upward its forecast of current profit growth for all industries in 1996/97 to 6.8 percent from 5.2 percent three months ago.

For the 1997/98 fiscal year, Nomura Research expects corporate profit growth of 5.8 percent, up from its previous forecast of 4.8 percent. Nikko Research revised up its previous 1997/98 corporate earnings forecast by 0.3 percentage point to 10.0 percent.
Daiwa Institute and Yamaichi Research revised down their forecasts for 1997/98.
Daiwa Institute said it saw 1997/98 corporate earnings growing by 9.0 percent, down from its previous forecast of 9.6 percent.
Yamaichi Research expects 1997/98 profits to grow by 10.3 percent, down from a prediction of 10.4 percent.
